Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas · Body, health & movement

forward adverb

towards the front, onward

also forwards, onward, go forward, step forward, back and forth

classical

Phaedr. 3.6.2: nōn vīs citius prōgredī?

prōgredior, prōgredī, prōgressus sum

verb, third conjugation, deponent

go forward, advance, go on

Latin puts “forward” into the verb with prō-: prōcēdere, step forward (illūc prōcēde, Plaut. Capt., Lewis & Short), prōgredī, go forward; and prōnus is “leaning forward” (Lewis & Short).

Examples

  • Quam tarda es! inquit; nōn vīs citius prōgredī?

    “How slow you are!” he said. “Won’t you get a move on?”Phaedr. 3.6.2

  • pergeret porrō īre nec ultrā inquīreret

    he was to keep going forward and ask no furtherLiv. 21.22.9

  • Trepidārī sentiō et cursārī rūrsum prōrsum.

    I can hear people bustling and running back and forth.Ter. Hec. 315

Other words

  • porrō — forward, onward, further on

    adverb · also used · classical · Liv. 21.22.9: pergeret porrō īre; Plaut. Amph. 803: perge porrō dīcere; de Vaan 481, s.v. por-: “straight on, forward, further”

    With verbs of going on, also of going on with a story: perge porrō, carry on.

  • prōrsum (prōrsus) — forwards

    adverb · also used · classical · Ter. Hec. 315: cursārī rūrsum prōrsum, “running back and forth”; Plaut. Cist. 4.2.32 (Lewis & Short)

    Mostly in comedy; rūrsum prōrsum is “back and forth”.

See also further, in front of, look forward to.

SourcesLewis & Short: progredior · Lewis & Short: procedo · Lewis & Short: porro · Lewis & Short: prorsum

Michiel de Vaan, Etymological Dictionary of Latin and the other Italic Languages (2008), p. 481.
